chunks: Hysteresis and Schmitt triggers. The question: What is hysteresis and why is it used?
Hysteresis means a circuit has two different switching points, depending on which way the input is moving. On the way up, the output flips at an upper threshold.
On the way down, it flips at a lower one. A Schmitt trigger is a circuit built this way.
It stops a noisy or slow input from making the output flicker near a single switching point.
Think of a home thermostat.
If it turned the heater on at exactly 70 degrees and off at exactly 70 degrees, the heater would click on and off all day as the temperature wobbled around 70.
So real thermostats turn the heater on at 68 and off at 72. That gap is the hysteresis.

Threshold: the input voltage at which a circuit's output flips. Hysteresis: the gap between the upper and lower thresholds. Schmitt trigger: a circuit or input with hysteresis.
Chatter: rapid repeated flipping of the output when a noisy input hovers near a threshold.
Positive feedback: sending part of the output back to the input so that it reinforces the output's current state. This is how the two thresholds are created.

33 volts. The output flips high once, when the input first passes 1. 815 volts. The 0. 1 volts noise cannot bring it back down to 1. 485 volts, so the output stays put.
That is the whole idea: a gap wider than the noise stops chatter.
"Hysteresis gives a circuit two thresholds: it switches high at an upper threshold when the input rises and low at a lower threshold when the input falls.
You build it with positive feedback, like feeding some of the comparator output back to the non-inverting input.
It's used so a slow or noisy input switches the output once instead of chattering around a single threshold.
The window must be bigger than the noise, and the trade-off is added delay and a dead band."
